headline: Russia and Ukraine pause fighting to help one town

sources.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say (BBC)
Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have 'frank' call with Putin (The Guardian)
Russia halts strikes on Ukraine's Kherson as Oleshky ceasefire takes effect (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: For the first time in years, the fighting around one small town in southern Ukraine has {{let up}}. A local [[truce]], an agreement to stop fighting for a set time, began there on October 27, 2026. It aims to get food, medicine and other [[aid]] to the people [[trapped]] in the town. Russian troops {{took over}} the town in the first days of Russia's [[invasion]] in February 2022. It sits across a river from a larger city that Ukraine [[controls]].

verbs.correct: To become weaker or stop for a while
verbs.wrong: To move closer to the river
verbs.why: The rain finally lets up in the late afternoon. The noise from the street never lets up on Saturday nights. For the first time in years, the fighting around the town has let up.

verbs.correct: To gain control of a place
verbs.wrong: To build walls around a town
verbs.why: A new owner takes over the old hotel and paints it blue. A big company takes over the empty factory and hires new workers. Russian troops took over the town in the first days of Russia's invasion in February 2022.

chunks.text: Before the war, about 24,000 people lived in the town. The United Nations says up to 2,000 [[remain]] today. Because of [[land mines]] and [[drone attacks]], the roads are too dangerous, so people cannot {{get out}}. The town has had no electricity, gas or [[running water]] since a nearby [[dam]] was destroyed in 2023. It is also {{cut off}} from regular food [[supplies]]. Stores there got their last food delivery in May.

verbs.wrong: To find enough food to eat
verbs.why: When the fire alarm rings, everyone gets out fast. Families get out before the floodwater reaches their street. Because of land mines and drone attacks, the people in the town cannot get out.

verbs.correct: To stop a place from getting supplies
verbs.wrong: To share food among many people
verbs.why: Heavy snow cuts the mountain village off from fresh food every winter. A big storm often cuts the island off from fuel deliveries. The town is also cut off from regular food supplies.

chunks.text: Melania Trump, the U.S. [[first lady]], and Pope Leo {{stepped in}} to help. Earlier in October, the pope {{reached out}} to the leaders of Russia and Ukraine about the town. The deal was [[announced]] on October 23, and both countries {{signed off on}} it. First, trucks will {{bring in}} doctors, medicine, food and water. Then [[evacuations]], when people are taken to safer places, are set to {{go ahead}} on Friday, October 30.

verbs.wrong: To give money for a cause
verbs.why: When two kids start a fight, a teacher steps in. A neighbor steps in when the family needs help with the baby. Melania Trump and Pope Leo stepped in to help the two sides agree.

verbs.correct: To contact someone to ask for something
verbs.wrong: To thank someone in a public speech
verbs.why: She reaches out to her old boss when she needs a job. The school reaches out to parents for help with the class trip. Earlier in October, the pope reached out to the leaders of Russia and Ukraine.

verbs.correct: To give official approval to something
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to decide
verbs.why: The manager signs off on every new hire. The city council signs off on the plan for a new park. Both Russia and Ukraine signed off on the deal.

verbs.correct: To deliver supplies to a place
verbs.why: Boats bring in fresh food to the island each week. Helicopters bring in water when the roads are closed. First, trucks will bring in doctors, medicine, food and water.

verbs.wrong: To be shown on the news
verbs.why: The game goes ahead even in light rain. The school trip goes ahead as planned. Evacuations are set to go ahead on Friday, October 30.

chunks.text: On October 27, the first lady said the truce now covers a wider area, so aid trucks can {{get through}} safely. Ukrainian officials {{backed up}} her statement. A spokesman for the Kremlin, Russia's government, said the truce was going [[according to plan]]. Ukraine's [[foreign minister]] said it could lead to more steps toward peace. Earlier attempts at a cease-fire {{fell through}} because of deep [[mistrust]]. The truce is due to last until late Sunday, November 1.

verbs.correct: To reach a place despite danger
verbs.wrong: To pay a fee at a checkpoint
verbs.why: Rescue boats get through the flood to reach families on their roofs. Only big trucks get through the icy mountain pass in winter. The truce now covers a wider area, so aid trucks can get through safely.

verbs.correct: To say that something is true
verbs.wrong: To ask someone to say it again
verbs.why: Photos back up her story about the accident. The numbers back up what the coach says about the team. Ukrainian officials backed up the first lady's statement.

verbs.wrong: To be kept secret from others
verbs.why: Sometimes a house sale falls through at the last minute. Our weekend plans fall through when my brother gets sick. Earlier attempts at a cease-fire fell through because of deep mistrust.

mainIdea.s: Russia and Ukraine stopped fighting around one small town so that help can arrive. Food, medicine and doctors go in first, and people who want to leave can then be taken to safer places.
mainIdea.why: The truce lets trucks bring in aid to people trapped in the town. After that, evacuations are set to go ahead for anyone who wants to leave.

mainIdea.s: A short truce in southern Ukraine is meant to empty a town of all of its residents first. When nobody is left there, aid groups will send food and doctors to start rebuilding it.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the aid comes first, and only people who want to leave will go. Trucks bring in doctors, medicine, food and water before the evacuations.

mainIdea.s: The leaders of Russia and Ukraine met in person and signed a full treaty that ends the war. Foreign soldiers are now going to guard a new border between the two countries for years.
mainIdea.why: There is no peace treaty. This is a short local truce that lets aid reach one town, and earlier cease-fire attempts fell through.

lines.text: Did you see that Russia and Ukraine agreed to a truce?
No, just around one small town in southern Ukraine. The fighting there has finally {{let up}}.
About 2,000 people are trapped there. Land mines and drones make it too dangerous to {{get out}}.
Do they at least have food?
Not much. The town is {{cut off}} from regular supplies, and stores got their last delivery in May.
Then help is [[long overdue]]. Who made the deal happen?
Melania Trump and Pope Leo {{stepped in}}. The pope {{reached out}} to both presidents in mid-October.
And both governments {{signed off on}} it?
Yes. First, trucks will {{bring in}} doctors, food and water. Then the evacuations should {{go ahead}} on Friday.
I bet people across the river breathed [[a sigh of relief]] too.
One woman there said the city feels a bit calmer. But are the aid trucks safe?
The first lady says the truce covers a wider area now, so they can {{get through}}. And Ukrainian officials {{backed up}} what she said.
That sounds like [[light at the end of the tunnel]].
Maybe. Earlier cease-fire plans {{fell through}} because of deep mistrust.
Me too. Whether it leads to real peace [[remains to be seen]].

expressions.expr: light at the end of the tunnel
expressions.def: A sign that a long, hard time is close to ending
ex: After months of treatment, she finally sees light at the end of the tunnel.

expressions.def: Used to say you feel hopeful but are careful not to expect too much
ex: The coach is cautiously optimistic about the new season.

expressions.def: Used to say that nobody knows the answer yet
